passages.title: Jeremiah receives his call
passages.summary: God appoints Jeremiah to speak to nations. Jeremiah objects that he is young and cannot speak.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches that God knew Jeremiah before birth. How does God answer Jeremiah’s fear about speaking?

contextNote.title: The call sets the book's two directions
contextNote.text: The verbs of destruction come before the verbs of planting and building. Jeremiah's task therefore includes both loss and a future beyond it. The visions develop that task before public speeches begin. His youth explains his objection, but it does not define the reach of his message.

passages.title: Broken water tanks and abandoned loyalty
passages.summary: Jeremiah recalls Israel’s early loyalty and later worship of other gods. He challenges reliance on Egypt and Assyria.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares God’s help with living water. What makes the broken water tanks poor replacements?

contextNote.title: A water image explains failed dependence
contextNote.text: The contrast places a living source beside containers that cannot retain water. It describes chosen replacements as inadequate to the need they must meet. Later references to Egypt and Assyria extend the question into political dependence. The chapter connects worship and alliances through that same problem.

passages.title: An invitation to return
passages.summary: God compares Israel and Judah with unfaithful wives. He calls scattered people to return and promises caring leaders.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s invitation to return. What must Israel acknowledge before accepting that invitation?

contextNote.title: One nation's failure does not excuse another
contextNote.text: Judah has witnessed Israel's breach and its consequences. The comparison therefore increases Judah's responsibility rather than proving its superiority. Calls to return follow the accusations. The marriage image describes the nations' loyalty. It is not a rule for judging women.

passages.title: An approaching enemy and a ruined land
passages.summary: Jeremiah warns of an army coming from the north. He pictures the land without light, people, or fruitful fields.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah describe the land as empty and dark?

contextNote.title: Destruction reverses the language of creation
contextNote.text: The vision removes light, people, birds, and fruitful land from the scene. Its sequence makes the threatened loss larger than defeat in battle. Jeremiah's bodily distress gives that vision a grieving witness. The passage joins warning with an account of what a ruined world would lose.

passages.title: A search for justice
passages.summary: Jeremiah searches Jerusalem for someone who acts justly. He finds wrongdoing among poor people, leaders, prophets, and priests.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does Jeremiah’s search change when he turns to powerful people?

contextNote.title: Knowledge of the law does not explain away injustice
contextNote.text: Jeremiah first expects leaders to understand what poor people may not know. Their conduct defeats that expectation. The search moves through social ranks rather than blaming one group alone. The later charges against prophets and priests make the failure a problem of public authority.

passages.title: Warnings that people refuse to hear
passages.summary: An enemy threatens Jerusalem. Leaders promise peace while people reject warnings and refuse to walk the older good path.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What damage follows the leaders’ promise of peace?

contextNote.title: Reassurance can conceal a wound
contextNote.text: The charge against leaders compares comforting speech with inadequate treatment of an injury. Calling the situation peaceful does not make the damage disappear. Warnings about deaf ears explain why correction fails to reach its hearers. The chapter tests speech by what it allows people to ignore.

passages.title: Temple worship and harm to neighbors
passages.summary: Jeremiah challenges people who trust the temple while harming others. Families also make offerings to the queen of the sky.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects temple worship with daily conduct. Which actions must change before the people can safely remain?

contextNote.title: A temple can become a false source of safety
contextNote.text: The warning targets trust in the temple’s name without changed conduct. Jeremiah connects worship with justice toward strangers, widows, and children without fathers. He also names theft, killing, and other gods. The building cannot protect a community that ignores these duties. Read the speech as a challenge to public habits, not only private belief.

passages.title: Rejected warnings and grief for the wounded
passages.summary: Jeremiah describes people refusing to return and scribes distorting the law. He grieves as harvest ends without deliverance.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah ask about medicine when describing his people’s wounds?

contextNote.title: Possessing written law does not secure right judgment
contextNote.text: The claim about scribes challenges confidence in the handling of the law itself. The chapter connects that confidence with refusal to return. Jeremiah's grief then gives the human cost a voice. Read the questions about healing beside the failure of those who claim to know.

passages.title: Broken trust and reasons for grief
passages.summary: Jeremiah mourns a people who lie and betray neighbors. He urges boasting in knowing God rather than wealth or strength.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What replaces wealth, wisdom, and strength as a reason for praise?

contextNote.title: Knowing God receives a practical definition
contextNote.text: The passage names kindness, justice, and righteousness after rejecting boasts of wealth and strength. Those actions answer the surrounding descriptions of deceit and unsafe relationships. Knowledge is measured through conduct that others experience. The chapter moves from broken public trust to the terms on which trust might return.

passages.title: Made idols and the living God
passages.summary: Jeremiah contrasts idols made from wood and metal with God. He mourns ruined homes and asks for measured correction.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the need to carry an idol support Jeremiah’s argument?

contextNote.title: Craftsmanship and authority are different claims
contextNote.text: The description follows cutting, shaping, fastening, and carrying an object. Those human actions expose the idol's dependence on its makers. The chapter then turns to ruined tents and scattered children. Its argument about trust sits beside a community whose ordinary supports are failing.

passages.title: A broken covenant and threats from Anathoth
passages.summary: God condemns Judah’s broken agreement and worship of Baal. Jeremiah learns that people from Anathoth plan to kill him.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does the threat from Anathoth make Jeremiah’s task harder?

contextNote.title: The speaker's own community tries to restrict his speech
contextNote.text: The threats arise in Anathoth, not only at the royal court. Familiar relationships therefore offer no automatic protection from opposition. The demand for silence turns a public covenant dispute into personal danger. Jeremiah's response brings the cost of speaking into the book's account.

passages.title: Jeremiah questions the success of wrongdoers
passages.summary: Jeremiah asks why dishonest people prosper. God warns about betrayal within his family and describes the ruined land.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the warning about Jeremiah’s family answer his complaint?

contextNote.title: A complaint tests the gap between justice and experience
contextNote.text: Jeremiah addresses God as righteous before asking why wrongdoers prosper. His question comes from observed conduct, not rejection of all justice. The answer warns of greater strain rather than immediate protection. Personal betrayal and a damaged land then widen the complaint beyond his own safety.

passages.title: A ruined waistband and stubborn habits
passages.summary: Jeremiah buries a linen waistband and retrieves it ruined. God compares Judah’s pride and stubborn conduct with ruined cloth.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What does the waistband’s change explain about Judah’s broken loyalty?

contextNote.title: A close-fitting object represents a broken relationship
contextNote.text: The linen belt belongs next to its wearer rather than at a distance. Its ruined condition makes lost closeness and usefulness visible. The act gives physical form to the chapter's accusation of pride. The later comparisons concern stubborn habits, not a moral ranking of skin colors.

passages.title: Drought and competing messages
passages.summary: Drought leaves people and animals without water. Jeremiah pleads for help while other prophets deny coming war and hunger.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How do the prophets’ promises differ from Jeremiah’s warning?

contextNote.title: Competing messages appear during visible scarcity
contextNote.text: The drought description begins with failed searches for water and suffering animals. Jeremiah's report of reassuring prophets follows that scene. Their promised peace must be read against conditions already shown to the reader. The conflict concerns whose words can be trusted during a public emergency.

passages.title: Jeremiah’s suffering and renewed task
passages.summary: God rejects further pleading for Judah and recalls Manasseh’s wrongdoing. Jeremiah describes isolation and receives a renewed charge to speak.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What must Jeremiah change when God renews his charge?

contextNote.title: The prophet's complaint is part of his service
contextNote.text: Jeremiah describes isolation and pain within his speech to God. The account does not reserve distress for people who reject the message. His renewed charge answers that complaint without promising public approval. Read his return to speaking beside the cost that made him question it.

passages.title: Missing celebrations and pursuing hunters
passages.summary: God forbids Jeremiah to marry or join mourning and feasts. He describes scattering, return, and fishers and hunters pursuing people.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses fishers and hunters to discuss gathering Israel. How does that lesson differ from the pursuit described in verses 16–18?

contextNote.title: Missing household rituals make coming loss visible
contextNote.text: Marriage, mourning, and feasting normally place a person within community life. Jeremiah's absence from them becomes part of his message. The restrictions describe losses that the wider people will soon experience. His body and daily habits carry a warning alongside his spoken words.

passages.title: Trust, hidden motives, and the Sabbath
passages.summary: Jeremiah contrasts trust in human strength with trust in God. He warns against carrying burdens through Jerusalem’s gates on the Sabbath.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the tree beside water remain fruitful during heat?

contextNote.title: The tree image allows difficulty within trust
contextNote.text: The tree remains fruitful while heat and drought still occur. Trust therefore changes its resources rather than removing adverse conditions. Later instructions about Sabbath burdens bring dependence into work and trade. The chapter connects hidden motives with choices visible at the city's gates.

passages.title: A potter’s work and plots against Jeremiah
passages.summary: Jeremiah watches a potter remake spoiled clay. Opponents plan to silence him, and he asks God to punish them.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the potter’s work. What does the spoiled clay’s new form explain about changing conduct?

contextNote.title: Soft clay presents a future that can change
contextNote.text: The potter can remake material that has not yet hardened. The explanation connects a nation's changed conduct with a changed outcome. The opponents' plans then show resistance to that possibility. Jeremiah's angry prayer belongs to the conflict that follows the teaching, not the potter's explanation.

passages.title: A broken jar before the elders
passages.summary: Jeremiah takes elders to the Hinnom Valley and breaks a jar. He condemns child sacrifice and warns of siege and death.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the broken jar differ from the clay in chapter 18?

contextNote.title: A broken vessel changes the force of the earlier image
contextNote.text: The jar differs from the soft clay in chapter 18. Once broken, it cannot simply return to its previous form. Taking elders as witnesses makes the action public. The warning presents a limit to the opportunity for change described in the earlier scene.

passages.title: Pashhur attacks Jeremiah
passages.summary: Pashhur strikes Jeremiah and puts him in stocks. Jeremiah warns him of exile, praises God, and curses his own birth.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Jeremiah’s costly service. Why can he neither stop speaking nor escape his grief?

contextNote.title: Praise and anguish remain in the same voice
contextNote.text: Jeremiah describes a message he cannot contain despite humiliation. The chapter moves from that pressure to praise and then a curse on his birth. These shifts prevent a smooth account of successful service. His confidence in rescue does not remove his suffering from the book.

passages.title: Zedekiah asks for rescue
passages.summary: Zedekiah sends Pashhur and Zephaniah to ask about Babylon’s attack. Jeremiah says surrender offers life while resistance brings death.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What answer challenges Zedekiah’s hope for a miraculous rescue?

contextNote.title: A request for rescue meets a demand for justice
contextNote.text: The royal delegation seeks help against an approaching army. Jeremiah's answer includes the ruler's duty to protect people from oppression. Military danger does not make domestic injustice irrelevant. The offered way to survive also conflicts with the king's hope for a restored victory.

passages.title: Kings judged by their treatment of others
passages.summary: Jeremiah condemns unpaid labor and violence under Judah’s kings. He contrasts Jehoiakim’s grand house with Josiah’s care for poor people.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah compare Jehoiakim’s cedar house with Josiah’s care for poor people?

contextNote.title: Royal buildings reveal how power treats workers
contextNote.text: The accusation concerns a fine house built through unpaid labor. Cedar and size cannot supply the justice missing from its construction. Josiah's treatment of poor people gives the comparison its alternative measure. The chapter judges royal achievement through the people who bear its cost.

passages.title: Harmful leaders and prophets who promise peace
passages.summary: God condemns leaders who scatter people and promises a just ruler. Jeremiah challenges prophets who give false comfort and report invented dreams.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What effect should a prophet’s words have on people’s conduct?

contextNote.title: A prophet's effect on conduct matters
contextNote.text: The critique links false reassurance with continued wrongdoing. A claim to speak for God cannot be tested by comfort alone. The chapter asks whether speech turns people from harm. Its promised ruler answers the scattered people's need for justice rather than another impressive title.

passages.title: Two baskets of figs
passages.summary: God compares deported Judeans with good figs. He compares Zedekiah and those left in Judah or Egypt with spoiled figs.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How do the good figs challenge assumptions about those taken to Babylon?

contextNote.title: Remaining at home does not prove divine favor
contextNote.text: The good figs represent people already taken away. That choice reverses an easy equation between survival in Judah and security. The promise of rebuilding reaches the displaced group. The vision therefore changes whose experience can carry the community's future.

passages.title: Babylon’s rule and the cup of anger
passages.summary: Jeremiah recounts twenty-three years of ignored warnings. He announces seventy years of Babylonian rule and judgment against many nations.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Babylon face judgment after serving God’s announced purpose?

contextNote.title: The conqueror also comes under judgment
contextNote.text: Babylon's announced role does not place it outside the wider warning. Its own punishment follows the period assigned to its rule. The cup then extends the scene to other nations. Read Judah's loss within that wider account without treating conquest as innocence.

passages.title: Jeremiah faces a death charge
passages.summary: Priests and prophets demand Jeremiah’s death after his temple warning. Officials spare him, while Jehoiakim has another prophet, Uriah, killed.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the memory of Micah help Jeremiah when Uriah receives no protection?

contextNote.title: Earlier prophecy becomes evidence in a public hearing
contextNote.text: The elders recall Micah when officials consider the demand for Jeremiah's death. That memory provides an alternative response to an unwelcome warning. Uriah's different fate prevents the hearing from becoming a universal promise of safety. Similar speech can meet different exercises of royal power.

passages.title: A yoke warns against rebellion
passages.summary: Jeremiah wears a wooden yoke and urges rulers to serve Babylon. He rejects promises that temple vessels will soon return.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah treat accepting the yoke as a way to survive?

contextNote.title: An object challenges the hope for immediate independence
contextNote.text: The yoke makes foreign service visible as a burden. Jeremiah directs the warning to rulers weighing resistance. The dispute about temple vessels connects political hope with sacred property. Preserving life, in this message, requires accepting a condition the audience wants to remove.

passages.title: Hananiah breaks the yoke
passages.summary: Hananiah promises return within two years and breaks Jeremiah’s wooden yoke. Jeremiah answers with an iron yoke, and Hananiah dies.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What does Jeremiah’s iron yoke answer in Hananiah’s promise?

contextNote.title: Breaking a symbol does not settle a dispute
contextNote.text: Hananiah's action dramatizes his promise of a swift return. Jeremiah distinguishes that promise from evidence of its fulfillment. The replacement iron yoke increases the warning's force. The chapter tests an attractive message through events rather than the confidence of its speaker.

passages.title: A letter to people in exile
passages.summary: Jeremiah tells captives to build homes and seek Babylon’s peace. He rejects other prophets’ claims and answers Shemaiah’s attempt to silence him.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah tell captives to pray for the city that holds them?

contextNote.title: A promise of return includes ordinary life in exile
contextNote.text: The letter names homes, gardens, marriages, and the city's peace. These duties assume a stay longer than the rival prophets promise. A hoped-for future does not cancel present work among foreign neighbors. Read the later promise beside these instructions for the years before it.

passages.title: Healing after national suffering
passages.summary: God promises Israel and Judah return, healing, and renewed life. He also says the nations that plundered them will face loss.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What does God promise people whom others call abandoned?

contextNote.title: Healing answers both injury and exclusion
contextNote.text: The charge that Zion is unwanted gives the wound a social dimension. Restoration must answer loss of belonging as well as damaged buildings. Former allies cannot provide that recovery. The chapter's reversal joins judgment on plunderers with a future for those they harmed.

passages.title: Return and a law written in hearts
passages.summary: God promises to gather scattered people and comfort Rachel’s grief. He announces a new covenant, an agreement with Israel and Judah.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s law written in hearts. How does the new agreement differ from the one the people broke?

contextNote.title: The covenant promise changes where the law resides
contextNote.text: The passage addresses Israel and Judah as peoples with a broken agreement. Writing in the heart contrasts with a relationship repeatedly violated. Forgiveness and shared knowledge accompany that change. Rachel's grief remains within the same chapter, placing renewed relation beside remembered loss.

passages.title: Jeremiah buys a field during the siege
passages.summary: While confined during the siege, Jeremiah buys Hanamel’s field in Anathoth. He gives the deeds to Baruch and questions the purchase.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s lasting promises. Why does Jeremiah preserve purchase deeds while Jerusalem faces capture?

contextNote.title: A land purchase gives hope a material form
contextNote.text: Jeremiah buys land while the city faces destruction. Witnesses, payment, copies, and storage make the purchase a public act. Preserving the deed assumes a future in which ownership can matter again. Hope here takes the form of a transaction during danger. The tablet offers an earlier regional comparison for recording land sales.

passages.title: Healing, a just ruler, and renewed worship
passages.summary: God promises to heal Jerusalem and restore joy and worship. He promises a just ruler from David’s family and continued priestly service.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me identifies the righteous Branch with Jesus Christ. What actions does the promised ruler perform?

contextNote.title: Restoration receives the sounds of ordinary life
contextNote.text: Wedding voices and thanksgiving replace the silence described around the city. Shepherds counting flocks give the promise another daily task. The future is more than repaired walls. Its picture of justice includes households, work, and worship that can continue together.

passages.title: Freed servants are forced back into slavery
passages.summary: Jerusalem’s owners release Hebrew servants under an agreement. They then force them back into service, and Jeremiah announces punishment.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does forcing freed servants back into slavery break the agreement?

contextNote.title: A public promise loses meaning when power reverses it
contextNote.text: The owners first agree to release their servants. Taking them back exposes the difference between a ceremony and sustained freedom. The charge names the people whose choices were removed. The siege does not excuse violating an agreement made before God.

passages.title: The Rechabites refuse wine
passages.summary: Jeremiah offers wine to the Rechabites, who refuse it. They explain their ancestor Jonadab’s commands and their move into Jerusalem for safety.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the Rechabites’ refusal challenge Judah’s response to God?

contextNote.title: A family tradition creates a comparison, not a universal rule
contextNote.text: The Rechabites explain whose command they preserve and why they entered the city. Their obedience contrasts with Judah's refusal of repeated divine messages. The comparison depends on keeping a received instruction. It does not require every reader to adopt all of that family's habits.

passages.title: Jehoiakim burns the scroll
passages.summary: Baruch writes and reads Jeremiah’s warnings. Jehoiakim burns the scroll despite objections, and Jeremiah dictates another scroll with added words.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies scripture that calls people to change. How does Jehoiakim’s response differ from the officials’ fear?

contextNote.title: Destroying a copy does not end the message
contextNote.text: The scroll moves through writing, public reading, court officials, and the king. Each stage changes who can hear its words. The king burns the copy as it is read. The command to write again answers that attempt to silence it. The chapter makes the survival of words part of the conflict.

passages.title: A false charge sends Jeremiah to prison
passages.summary: Babylon’s troops withdraw when Egypt’s army approaches. Irijah accuses Jeremiah of joining the enemy, and officials imprison him despite his denial.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the cost of following prophetic counsel. Why does Zedekiah seek Jeremiah’s answer secretly?

contextNote.title: A temporary change in the war encourages a false conclusion
contextNote.text: Babylon's withdrawal creates hope that the threat has ended. Jeremiah challenges that reading while facing accusations of desertion. The king then seeks information privately from the prisoner. The account separates visible movement, political expectation, and the warning that continues despite both.

passages.title: Ebedmelech rescues Jeremiah
passages.summary: Officials lower Jeremiah into a muddy pit. Ebedmelech secures help and rescues him, while Zedekiah privately asks about surrender.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Ebedmelech’s courage. What risks does he accept when he asks the king to rescue Jeremiah?

contextNote.title: Practical care answers danger that official power created
contextNote.text: The rescue includes worn cloth to protect Jeremiah under the ropes. That small detail makes Ebedmelech's intervention more than a request for mercy. The king permits rescue but still fears following the prophet's advice. Helpful authority in one decision does not resolve his larger refusal.

passages.title: Jerusalem falls and Jeremiah is spared
passages.summary: Babylon captures Jerusalem and Zedekiah. The invaders kill his sons and blind him. Jeremiah receives protection, and Ebedmelech receives a promise of survival.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies choices made during danger. How does Ebedmelech’s response differ from Zedekiah’s earlier fear?

contextNote.title: The city's fall affects people in unequal ways
contextNote.text: The royal household suffers capture and severe punishment. Some poor people receive land while others are removed. The account does not make conquest one uniform experience. Jeremiah's protection and Ebedmelech's promise form further distinct outcomes within the same disaster.

passages.title: Gedaliah governs the remaining people
passages.summary: Nebuzaradan frees Jeremiah, who stays with Gedaliah at Mizpah. Judeans return to harvest, but Gedaliah rejects a warning about Ishmael.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Johanan think Ishmael’s plan threatens everyone gathered around Gedaliah?

contextNote.title: Harvest work offers a fragile recovery after conquest
contextNote.text: Gedaliah's invitation focuses on gathering produce and living in towns. That ordinary work contrasts with the preceding siege and removal. The warning about Ishmael threatens the limited safety needed for recovery. Refusing to believe it leaves the community's future exposed.

passages.title: Ishmael kills Gedaliah and takes captives
passages.summary: Ishmael kills Gedaliah and visiting mourners, then takes captives. Johanan recovers the captives, and Ishmael escapes toward Ammon.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How do Ishmael’s killings change the survivors’ plans for staying in Judah?

contextNote.title: A local killing changes the survivors' political choices
contextNote.text: Gedaliah's death destroys the arrangement under which farming had resumed. Fear of Babylon's response then shapes the recovered captives' next decision. Their danger comes through events inside the remaining community. The movement toward Egypt grows from that fear before they request divine guidance.

passages.title: Survivors ask for guidance
passages.summary: Johanan and the survivors promise to obey God’s answer. Jeremiah tells them to remain in Judah and warns against seeking safety in Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What part of the survivors’ promise becomes difficult when Jeremiah gives the answer?

contextNote.title: A promise to obey is tested by an unwanted answer
contextNote.text: The survivors agree to accept either a pleasing or difficult response. Jeremiah's answer challenges the destination they already consider safer. The ten-day wait also prevents an immediate endorsement of their plan. The account places declared obedience beside the concrete choice that will test it.

passages.title: The survivors reject the answer
passages.summary: Johanan and Azariah accuse Jeremiah of lying and blame Baruch. They take the survivors, Jeremiah, and Baruch into Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does blaming Baruch help the leaders reject Jeremiah’s message?

contextNote.title: An accusation replaces an answer to the warning
contextNote.text: The leaders blame Baruch for directing Jeremiah's speech. That claim shifts attention from the message to an alleged hidden motive. They then take the group into Egypt despite the warning. The buried stones give the new destination a danger they expected to escape.

passages.title: A dispute about the queen of the sky
passages.summary: Judeans in Egypt insist that their goddess offerings brought prosperity. Jeremiah says those offerings caused the ruin they seek to escape.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How do the women and Jeremiah explain the lost food and peace differently?

contextNote.title: The dispute concerns the remembered cause of disaster
contextNote.text: The people associate prosperity with their earlier offerings. Jeremiah interprets those same practices as the cause of destruction. Both speakers use memory to explain the present loss. The text records competing claims without giving the queen of the sky a personal name.

passages.title: Baruch receives a promise of survival
passages.summary: Baruch laments his added sorrow and lack of rest. God warns him against seeking greatness and promises that he will keep his life.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What does Baruch receive instead of the greatness he seeks?

contextNote.title: A scribe's private hopes meet a public crisis
contextNote.text: Baruch's complaint gives the person who writes the message his own voice. The answer places his hopes within the destruction facing the land. Survival replaces the greatness he might seek. His sorrow is acknowledged without a promise that serving the message brings personal advancement.

passages.title: Egypt’s armies face defeat
passages.summary: Jeremiah describes Egypt’s defeat at Carchemish and warns of invasion. He also promises that scattered Israel will not be abandoned.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does Egypt’s boast differ from the soldiers’ flight?

contextNote.title: A river image exposes the gap between boast and outcome
contextNote.text: Egypt describes its advance as water covering the land. The battle scene turns that confidence into panic and retreat. Many troops do not guarantee the power claimed by the image. The final promise to Israel gives the chapter a second audience beyond the defeated army.

passages.title: A warning against the Philistines
passages.summary: Jeremiah describes destruction reaching Philistine cities and their helpers. A voice asks when the sword will finally rest.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does the passage ask the sword to rest?

contextNote.title: A question asks how long violence will continue
contextNote.text: The request for rest interrupts the announcement of destruction. It asks about the duration of violence rather than celebrating an enemy's loss. The answering voice keeps the announced judgment in view. The exchange lets grief and warning occupy the same short poem.

passages.title: Moab’s pride and suffering
passages.summary: Jeremiah announces destruction across Moab and captivity for Chemosh’s worshipers. He mourns ruined vineyards and ends with a promise of return.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the mourning for Moab complicate the warning against its pride?

contextNote.title: Grief remains beside the charge against Moab
contextNote.text: The speaker mourns the people whose pride the warning condemns. Ruined vineyards turn national loss into damage to familiar work and celebration. That sorrow complicates a reading based only on punishment. The closing return promise also prevents destruction from being the chapter's final word.

passages.title: Warnings against neighboring peoples
passages.summary: Jeremiah announces judgment against Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Hazor, and Elam. Promises of later return accompany warnings for Ammon and Elam.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Which kinds of protection fail in these warnings?

contextNote.title: Different neighbors receive different endings
contextNote.text: The warnings address several peoples with distinct sources of confidence. Wealth, high places, and weapons fail in different scenes. Return promises appear for Ammon and Elam, but not for every named people. Keep those differences when reading the chapter as a group of national warnings.

passages.title: Babylon faces judgment
passages.summary: Jeremiah announces Babylon’s fall and urges captives to leave. He promises Israel and Judah return, forgiveness, and a renewed agreement with God.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Babylon remain responsible after serving as an instrument of judgment?

contextNote.title: Being used in judgment does not excuse violence
contextNote.text: The attackers claim innocence because their victims had sinned. The warning against Babylon rejects that escape from responsibility. Israel and Judah's promised return therefore includes judgment on their captor. The book does not give one power permanent immunity because it once served a purpose.

passages.title: A scroll marks Babylon’s announced fall
passages.summary: Jeremiah continues the warning against Babylon. He tells Seraiah to read a scroll there and sink it in the Euphrates.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah tell Seraiah to sink the scroll after reading it?

contextNote.title: Reading and sinking make a message into a witnessed act
contextNote.text: Seraiah must first read the warning in Babylon. A stone then sends the scroll beneath the river's surface. The spoken explanation gives that action its meaning. The act presents an announced future, not a record that Babylon had already fallen.

passages.title: Jerusalem’s destruction and Jehoiachin’s release
passages.summary: The closing account describes Jerusalem’s siege, destruction, executions, and forced removal of captives. Years later, Evilmerodach frees Jehoiachin and gives him a daily allowance.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What changes for Jehoiachin, and what losses remain unchanged?

contextNote.title: The appendix keeps a surviving king beside an unrepaired loss
contextNote.text: The detailed destruction follows Jeremiah's speeches rather than ending with their promises. Temple objects, officials, and captives all enter its record of loss. Jehoiachin's later release changes one person's treatment. It offers a surviving royal line without claiming the temple or kingdom has returned.

events.title: Jeremiah receives his call
events.summary: God appoints Jeremiah to speak to nations. Jeremiah objects that he is young and cannot speak.
events.detail: The verbs of destruction come before the verbs of planting and building. Jeremiah's task therefore includes both loss and a future beyond it. The visions develop that task before public speeches begin. His youth explains his objection, but it does not define the reach of his message.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches that God knew Jeremiah before birth. How does God answer Jeremiah’s fear about speaking?

events.title: Broken water tanks and abandoned loyalty
events.summary: Jeremiah recalls Israel’s early loyalty and later worship of other gods. He challenges reliance on Egypt and Assyria.
events.detail: The contrast places a living source beside containers that cannot retain water. It describes chosen replacements as inadequate to the need they must meet. Later references to Egypt and Assyria extend the question into political dependence. The chapter connects worship and alliances through that same problem.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares God’s help with living water. What makes the broken water tanks poor replacements?

events.title: An invitation to return
events.summary: God compares Israel and Judah with unfaithful wives. He calls scattered people to return and promises caring leaders.
events.detail: Judah has witnessed Israel's breach and its consequences. The comparison therefore increases Judah's responsibility rather than proving its superiority. Calls to return follow the accusations. The marriage image describes the nations' loyalty. It is not a rule for judging women.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s invitation to return. What must Israel acknowledge before accepting that invitation?

events.title: An approaching enemy and a ruined land
events.summary: Jeremiah warns of an army coming from the north. He pictures the land without light, people, or fruitful fields.
events.detail: The vision removes light, people, birds, and fruitful land from the scene. Its sequence makes the threatened loss larger than defeat in battle. Jeremiah's bodily distress gives that vision a grieving witness. The passage joins warning with an account of what a ruined world would lose.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah describe the land as empty and dark?

events.title: A search for justice
events.summary: Jeremiah searches Jerusalem for someone who acts justly. He finds wrongdoing among poor people, leaders, prophets, and priests.
events.detail: Jeremiah first expects leaders to understand what poor people may not know. Their conduct defeats that expectation. The search moves through social ranks rather than blaming one group alone. The later charges against prophets and priests make the failure a problem of public authority.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does Jeremiah’s search change when he turns to powerful people?

events.title: Warnings that people refuse to hear
events.summary: An enemy threatens Jerusalem. Leaders promise peace while people reject warnings and refuse to walk the older good path.
events.detail: The charge against leaders compares comforting speech with inadequate treatment of an injury. Calling the situation peaceful does not make the damage disappear. Warnings about deaf ears explain why correction fails to reach its hearers. The chapter tests speech by what it allows people to ignore.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What damage follows the leaders’ promise of peace?

events.title: Temple worship and harm to neighbors
events.summary: Jeremiah challenges people who trust the temple while harming others. Families also make offerings to the queen of the sky.
events.detail: The warning targets trust in the temple’s name without changed conduct. Jeremiah connects worship with justice toward strangers, widows, and children without fathers. He also names theft, killing, and other gods. The building cannot protect a community that ignores these duties. Read the speech as a challenge to public habits, not only private belief.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects temple worship with daily conduct. Which actions must change before the people can safely remain?

events.title: Rejected warnings and grief for the wounded
events.summary: Jeremiah describes people refusing to return and scribes distorting the law. He grieves as harvest ends without deliverance.
events.detail: The claim about scribes challenges confidence in the handling of the law itself. The chapter connects that confidence with refusal to return. Jeremiah's grief then gives the human cost a voice. Read the questions about healing beside the failure of those who claim to know.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah ask about medicine when describing his people’s wounds?

events.title: Broken trust and reasons for grief
events.summary: Jeremiah mourns a people who lie and betray neighbors. He urges boasting in knowing God rather than wealth or strength.
events.detail: The passage names kindness, justice, and righteousness after rejecting boasts of wealth and strength. Those actions answer the surrounding descriptions of deceit and unsafe relationships. Knowledge is measured through conduct that others experience. The chapter moves from broken public trust to the terms on which trust might return.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What replaces wealth, wisdom, and strength as a reason for praise?

events.title: Made idols and the living God
events.summary: Jeremiah contrasts idols made from wood and metal with God. He mourns ruined homes and asks for measured correction.
events.detail: The description follows cutting, shaping, fastening, and carrying an object. Those human actions expose the idol's dependence on its makers. The chapter then turns to ruined tents and scattered children. Its argument about trust sits beside a community whose ordinary supports are failing.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the need to carry an idol support Jeremiah’s argument?

events.title: A broken covenant and threats from Anathoth
events.summary: God condemns Judah’s broken agreement and worship of Baal. Jeremiah learns that people from Anathoth plan to kill him.
events.detail: The threats arise in Anathoth, not only at the royal court. Familiar relationships therefore offer no automatic protection from opposition. The demand for silence turns a public covenant dispute into personal danger. Jeremiah's response brings the cost of speaking into the book's account.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does the threat from Anathoth make Jeremiah’s task harder?

events.title: Jeremiah questions the success of wrongdoers
events.summary: Jeremiah asks why dishonest people prosper. God warns about betrayal within his family and describes the ruined land.
events.detail: Jeremiah addresses God as righteous before asking why wrongdoers prosper. His question comes from observed conduct, not rejection of all justice. The answer warns of greater strain rather than immediate protection. Personal betrayal and a damaged land then widen the complaint beyond his own safety.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the warning about Jeremiah’s family answer his complaint?

events.title: A ruined waistband and stubborn habits
events.summary: Jeremiah buries a linen waistband and retrieves it ruined. God compares Judah’s pride and stubborn conduct with ruined cloth.
events.detail: The linen belt belongs next to its wearer rather than at a distance. Its ruined condition makes lost closeness and usefulness visible. The act gives physical form to the chapter's accusation of pride. The later comparisons concern stubborn habits, not a moral ranking of skin colors.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What does the waistband’s change explain about Judah’s broken loyalty?

events.title: Drought and competing messages
events.summary: Drought leaves people and animals without water. Jeremiah pleads for help while other prophets deny coming war and hunger.
events.detail: The drought description begins with failed searches for water and suffering animals. Jeremiah's report of reassuring prophets follows that scene. Their promised peace must be read against conditions already shown to the reader. The conflict concerns whose words can be trusted during a public emergency.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How do the prophets’ promises differ from Jeremiah’s warning?

events.title: Jeremiah’s suffering and renewed task
events.summary: God rejects further pleading for Judah and recalls Manasseh’s wrongdoing. Jeremiah describes isolation and receives a renewed charge to speak.
events.detail: Jeremiah describes isolation and pain within his speech to God. The account does not reserve distress for people who reject the message. His renewed charge answers that complaint without promising public approval. Read his return to speaking beside the cost that made him question it.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What must Jeremiah change when God renews his charge?

events.title: Missing celebrations and pursuing hunters
events.summary: God forbids Jeremiah to marry or join mourning and feasts. He describes scattering, return, and fishers and hunters pursuing people.
events.detail: Marriage, mourning, and feasting normally place a person within community life. Jeremiah's absence from them becomes part of his message. The restrictions describe losses that the wider people will soon experience. His body and daily habits carry a warning alongside his spoken words.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses fishers and hunters to discuss gathering Israel. How does that lesson differ from the pursuit described in verses 16–18?

events.title: Trust, hidden motives, and the Sabbath
events.summary: Jeremiah contrasts trust in human strength with trust in God. He warns against carrying burdens through Jerusalem’s gates on the Sabbath.
events.detail: The tree remains fruitful while heat and drought still occur. Trust therefore changes its resources rather than removing adverse conditions. Later instructions about Sabbath burdens bring dependence into work and trade. The chapter connects hidden motives with choices visible at the city's gates.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the tree beside water remain fruitful during heat?

events.title: A potter’s work and plots against Jeremiah
events.summary: Jeremiah watches a potter remake spoiled clay. Opponents plan to silence him, and he asks God to punish them.
events.detail: The potter can remake material that has not yet hardened. The explanation connects a nation's changed conduct with a changed outcome. The opponents' plans then show resistance to that possibility. Jeremiah's angry prayer belongs to the conflict that follows the teaching, not the potter's explanation.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the potter’s work. What does the spoiled clay’s new form explain about changing conduct?

events.title: A broken jar before the elders
events.summary: Jeremiah takes elders to the Hinnom Valley and breaks a jar. He condemns child sacrifice and warns of siege and death.
events.detail: The jar differs from the soft clay in chapter 18. Once broken, it cannot simply return to its previous form. Taking elders as witnesses makes the action public. The warning presents a limit to the opportunity for change described in the earlier scene.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the broken jar differ from the clay in chapter 18?

events.title: Pashhur attacks Jeremiah
events.summary: Pashhur strikes Jeremiah and puts him in stocks. Jeremiah warns him of exile, praises God, and curses his own birth.
events.detail: Jeremiah describes a message he cannot contain despite humiliation. The chapter moves from that pressure to praise and then a curse on his birth. These shifts prevent a smooth account of successful service. His confidence in rescue does not remove his suffering from the book.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Jeremiah’s costly service. Why can he neither stop speaking nor escape his grief?

events.title: Zedekiah asks for rescue
events.summary: Zedekiah sends Pashhur and Zephaniah to ask about Babylon’s attack. Jeremiah says surrender offers life while resistance brings death.
events.detail: The royal delegation seeks help against an approaching army. Jeremiah's answer includes the ruler's duty to protect people from oppression. Military danger does not make domestic injustice irrelevant. The offered way to survive also conflicts with the king's hope for a restored victory.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What answer challenges Zedekiah’s hope for a miraculous rescue?

events.title: Kings judged by their treatment of others
events.summary: Jeremiah condemns unpaid labor and violence under Judah’s kings. He contrasts Jehoiakim’s grand house with Josiah’s care for poor people.
events.detail: The accusation concerns a fine house built through unpaid labor. Cedar and size cannot supply the justice missing from its construction. Josiah's treatment of poor people gives the comparison its alternative measure. The chapter judges royal achievement through the people who bear its cost.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah compare Jehoiakim’s cedar house with Josiah’s care for poor people?

events.title: Harmful leaders and prophets who promise peace
events.summary: God condemns leaders who scatter people and promises a just ruler. Jeremiah challenges prophets who give false comfort and report invented dreams.
events.detail: The critique links false reassurance with continued wrongdoing. A claim to speak for God cannot be tested by comfort alone. The chapter asks whether speech turns people from harm. Its promised ruler answers the scattered people's need for justice rather than another impressive title.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What effect should a prophet’s words have on people’s conduct?

events.title: Two baskets of figs
events.summary: God compares deported Judeans with good figs. He compares Zedekiah and those left in Judah or Egypt with spoiled figs.
events.detail: The good figs represent people already taken away. That choice reverses an easy equation between survival in Judah and security. The promise of rebuilding reaches the displaced group. The vision therefore changes whose experience can carry the community's future.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How do the good figs challenge assumptions about those taken to Babylon?

events.title: Babylon’s rule and the cup of anger
events.summary: Jeremiah recounts twenty-three years of ignored warnings. He announces seventy years of Babylonian rule and judgment against many nations.
events.detail: Babylon's announced role does not place it outside the wider warning. Its own punishment follows the period assigned to its rule. The cup then extends the scene to other nations. Read Judah's loss within that wider account without treating conquest as innocence.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Babylon face judgment after serving God’s announced purpose?

events.title: Jeremiah faces a death charge
events.summary: Priests and prophets demand Jeremiah’s death after his temple warning. Officials spare him, while Jehoiakim has another prophet, Uriah, killed.
events.detail: The elders recall Micah when officials consider the demand for Jeremiah's death. That memory provides an alternative response to an unwelcome warning. Uriah's different fate prevents the hearing from becoming a universal promise of safety. Similar speech can meet different exercises of royal power.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: How does the memory of Micah help Jeremiah when Uriah receives no protection?

events.title: A yoke warns against rebellion
events.summary: Jeremiah wears a wooden yoke and urges rulers to serve Babylon. He rejects promises that temple vessels will soon return.
events.detail: The yoke makes foreign service visible as a burden. Jeremiah directs the warning to rulers weighing resistance. The dispute about temple vessels connects political hope with sacred property. Preserving life, in this message, requires accepting a condition the audience wants to remove.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah treat accepting the yoke as a way to survive?

events.title: Hananiah breaks the yoke
events.summary: Hananiah promises return within two years and breaks Jeremiah’s wooden yoke. Jeremiah answers with an iron yoke, and Hananiah dies.
events.detail: Hananiah's action dramatizes his promise of a swift return. Jeremiah distinguishes that promise from evidence of its fulfillment. The replacement iron yoke increases the warning's force. The chapter tests an attractive message through events rather than the confidence of its speaker.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What does Jeremiah’s iron yoke answer in Hananiah’s promise?

events.title: A letter to people in exile
events.summary: Jeremiah tells captives to build homes and seek Babylon’s peace. He rejects other prophets’ claims and answers Shemaiah’s attempt to silence him.
events.detail: The letter names homes, gardens, marriages, and the city's peace. These duties assume a stay longer than the rival prophets promise. A hoped-for future does not cancel present work among foreign neighbors. Read the later promise beside these instructions for the years before it.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah tell captives to pray for the city that holds them?

events.title: Healing after national suffering
events.summary: God promises Israel and Judah return, healing, and renewed life. He also says the nations that plundered them will face loss.
events.detail: The charge that Zion is unwanted gives the wound a social dimension. Restoration must answer loss of belonging as well as damaged buildings. Former allies cannot provide that recovery. The chapter's reversal joins judgment on plunderers with a future for those they harmed.
events.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What does God promise people whom others call abandoned?

events.title: Return and a law written in hearts
events.summary: God promises to gather scattered people and comfort Rachel’s grief. He announces a new covenant, an agreement with Israel and Judah.
events.detail: The passage addresses Israel and Judah as peoples with a broken agreement. Writing in the heart contrasts with a relationship repeatedly violated. Forgiveness and shared knowledge accompany that change. Rachel's grief remains within the same chapter, placing renewed relation beside remembered loss.

events.detail: Wedding voices and thanksgiving replace the silence described around the city. Shepherds counting flocks give the promise another daily task. The future is more than repaired walls. Its picture of justice includes households, work, and worship that can continue together.

events.detail: The owners first agree to release their servants. Taking them back exposes the difference between a ceremony and sustained freedom. The charge names the people whose choices were removed. The siege does not excuse violating an agreement made before God.

events.detail: The warnings address several peoples with distinct sources of confidence. Wealth, high places, and weapons fail in different scenes. events.title: Babylon faces judgment
events.summary: Jeremiah announces Babylon’s fall and urges captives to leave. He promises Israel and Judah return, forgiveness, and a renewed agreement with God.
events.detail: The attackers claim innocence because their victims had sinned. The warning against Babylon rejects that escape from responsibility. Israel and Judah's promised return therefore includes judgment on their captor. The book does not give one power permanent immunity because it once served a purpose.

events.title: A scroll marks Babylon’s announced fall

events.detail: Seraiah must first read the warning in Babylon. A stone then sends the scroll beneath the river's surface. The spoken explanation gives that action its meaning. The act presents an announced future, not a record that Babylon had already fallen.

guides.title: Jeremiah: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A temple can become a false source of safety
steps.text: The warning targets trust in the temple’s name without changed conduct. Jeremiah connects worship with justice toward strangers, widows, and children without fathers. He also names theft, killing, and other gods. The building cannot protect a community that ignores these duties. Read the speech as a challenge to public habits, not only private belief.

steps.title: A land purchase gives hope a material form
steps.text: Jeremiah buys land while the city faces destruction. Witnesses, payment, copies, and storage make the purchase a public act. Preserving the deed assumes a future in which ownership can matter again. Hope here takes the form of a transaction during danger. The tablet offers an earlier regional comparison for recording land sales.

steps.title: Destroying a copy does not end the message
steps.text: The scroll moves through writing, public reading, court officials, and the king. Each stage changes who can hear its words. The king burns the copy as it is read. The command to write again answers that attempt to silence it. The chapter makes the survival of words part of the conflict.

textRoutes.title: A letter to people in exile
textRoutes.summary: Jeremiah tells captives to build homes and seek Babylon’s peace. He rejects other prophets’ claims and answers Shemaiah’s attempt to silence him.
textRoutes.detail: The letter names homes, gardens, marriages, and the city's peace. These duties assume a stay longer than the rival prophets promise. A hoped-for future does not cancel present work among foreign neighbors. Read the later promise beside these instructions for the years before it.
textRoutes.uncertainty: Jeremiah 29:1–3 describes Elasah and Gemariah delivering the letter from Jerusalem to captives in Babylon. Intermediate roads are not specified.
textRoutes.evidence: Jeremiah 29:1–3 describes Elasah and Gemariah delivering the letter from Jerusalem to captives in Babylon. Intermediate roads are not specified.

textRoutes.title: Jerusalem falls and Jeremiah is spared
textRoutes.summary: Babylon captures Jerusalem and Zedekiah. The invaders kill his sons and blind him. Jeremiah receives protection, and Ebedmelech receives a promise of survival.
textRoutes.detail: The royal household suffers capture and severe punishment. Some poor people receive land while others are removed. The account does not make conquest one uniform experience. Jeremiah's protection and Ebedmelech's promise form further distinct outcomes within the same disaster.
textRoutes.uncertainty: Jeremiah 39:4–7 traces Zedekiah’s escape, capture near Jericho, judgment at Riblah, and removal to Babylon. Lines connect approximate named locations, not known roads.
textRoutes.evidence: Jeremiah 39:4–7 traces Zedekiah’s escape, capture near Jericho, judgment at Riblah, and removal to Babylon. Lines connect approximate named locations, not known roads.

textRoutes.title: Gedaliah governs the remaining people
textRoutes.summary: Nebuzaradan frees Jeremiah, who stays with Gedaliah at Mizpah. Judeans return to harvest, but Gedaliah rejects a warning about Ishmael.
textRoutes.detail: Gedaliah's invitation focuses on gathering produce and living in towns. That ordinary work contrasts with the preceding siege and removal. The warning about Ishmael threatens the limited safety needed for recovery. Refusing to believe it leaves the community's future exposed.
textRoutes.uncertainty: Jeremiah 40:1–6 places Jeremiah among captives at Ramah and then with Gedaliah at Mizpah. The exact road and competing site locations remain uncertain.
textRoutes.evidence: Jeremiah 40:1–6 places Jeremiah among captives at Ramah and then with Gedaliah at Mizpah. The exact road and competing site locations remain uncertain.

textRoutes.title: Jerusalem’s destruction and Jehoiachin’s release
textRoutes.summary: The closing account describes Jerusalem’s siege, destruction, executions, and forced removal of captives. Years later, Evilmerodach frees Jehoiachin and gives him a daily allowance.
textRoutes.detail: The detailed destruction follows Jeremiah's speeches rather than ending with their promises. Temple objects, officials, and captives all enter its record of loss. Jehoiachin's later release changes one person's treatment. It offers a surviving royal line without claiming the temple or kingdom has returned.
